steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a robotics paper about a fast, batched distance checker that makes time-optimal safe path tracking of collaborative robots practical. Explain why current distance computation is not good enough for real-time safety control, summarize our method and results, and finish with how the paper is organized.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Working together with robots while keeping humans safe is a critical challenge, because if the robot is slowed down to avoid injuries then productivity suffers. To get the most productivity out of collaborative robots and still guarantee safety, we proposed a time-optimal path tracking algorithm that runs in real-time and gives the safe and fastest control input with respect to Speed and Separation Monitoring in ISO standards. For this path-tracking method the distances between the obstacles and the robot have to be given for the waypoints along the trajectory being executed. With these distances the algorithm computes the fastest velocity profile and the robot is navigated in a time-optimal way (Fig. 1). Then the control input is sent to the robot so that it follows the velocity profile. All of this has to run in every control cycle, which is about 10 \mathrm{m}\mathrm{s} because of the communication protocol of industrial robots.

For true optimality in path tracking, the distances have to be precise. In our previous paper we simplified the robot with spheres and computed the distances between the spheres and the voxels with the hypot function using their center positions. Distance checking with this simplified model can run almost in real-time. But because of the simplification the computed distances are smaller than the actual ones, so the robot behaves conservatively and its productivity gets worse. On the other hand, an exact mesh-to-mesh distance checker is not able to run in real-time (in our experiments 130 \mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro s} for one configuration and 65 \mathrm{m}\mathrm{s} for one trajectory with FCL). As far as we know, there is no existing distance checker that can be used for real-time safety control.

- Our proposal
  - batched, fast, precise distance checker on pre-computed link-local Signed Distance Fields (SDFs)
  - GPU parallelization for pre-processing robot SDFs; multiple configurations in less than 1 \mathrm{m}\mathrm{s} at runtime
  - neural approximation of pre-processing: 2x faster
  - experiment: navigates robot faster than sphere model, dynamic collaborative environment
- Organization
  - II related work; III parallel distance checking + constant-order pre-processing tricks incl. neural approximation
  - IV evaluation of neural approximation + precision; experimental comparison for real-time safe path tracking
  - V limitations, conclusion, future work

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Working together with robots while keeping humans safe is a critical challenge, because if the robot is slowed down to avoid injuries then productivity suffers. To get the most productivity out of collaborative robots and still guarantee safety, we proposed a time-optimal path tracking algorithm that runs in real-time and gives the safe and fastest control input with respect to Speed and Separation Monitoring in ISO standards. For this path-tracking method the distances between the obstacles and the robot have to be given for the waypoints along the trajectory being executed. With these distances the algorithm computes the fastest velocity profile and the robot is navigated in a time-optimal way (Fig. 1). Then the control input is sent to the robot so that it follows the velocity profile. All of this has to run in every control cycle, which is about 10 \mathrm{m}\mathrm{s} because of the communication protocol of industrial robots.

For true optimality in path tracking, the distances have to be precise. In our previous paper we simplified the robot with spheres and computed the distances between the spheres and the voxels with the hypot function using their center positions. Distance checking with this simplified model can run almost in real-time. But because of the simplification the computed distances are smaller than the actual ones, so the robot behaves conservatively and its productivity gets worse. On the other hand, an exact mesh-to-mesh distance checker is not able to run in real-time (in our experiments 130 \mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro s} for one configuration and 65 \mathrm{m}\mathrm{s} for one trajectory with FCL). As far as we know, there is no existing distance checker that can be used for real-time safety control.

In this paper we propose a distance checker that is batched, fast and precise, based on pre-computed link-local Signed Distance Fields (SDFs), to solve this problem. We use GPU parallelization for the pre-processing of the robot's SDFs, and with this the method can check distances for multiple robot configurations in less than 1 \mathrm{m}\mathrm{s} at runtime. We also propose a neural approximation of the pre-processing, which makes pre-processing 2x faster. Finally we show in experiments that our distance checker navigates a robot faster than the method that models the robot with spheres, in a dynamic, collaborative environment.

The rest of the paper is organized like this. Section II surveys related work. Section III presents our parallel distance checking method and also some techniques to reduce the pre-processing time in a constant order, including the neural approximation. Section IV evaluates the performance of the neural approximation and checks that the approximation does not affect the precision of the distance computation. After that we show the experimental comparison for real-time safe path tracking in a collaborative environment. Finally, in Section V we discuss the limitations of our approach and conclude with some directions for future work.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Collaborating with robots while ensuring human safety has been a critical challenge, since slowing down the robot operation to mitigate injuries impedes productivity. To maximize the productivity of collaborative robots while guaranteeing safety, we have proposed a time-optimal path tracking algorithm [1] which runs in real-time and provides the safe and fastest control input with respect to Speed and Separation Monitoring in ISO standards [2]. In this path-tracking method, the distances between the obstacles and the robot for waypoints along the executing trajectory must be given. Given the distances, the algorithm computes the fastest velocity profile and navigates the robot in a time-optimal manner (Fig. 1). Finally, the control input is sent to the robot to follow the derived velocity profile. This whole process must run in every control cycle, which is about 10 \mathrm{m}\mathrm{s} according to the communication protocol of industrial robots.

To achieve true optimality in path tracking, precise distances need to be given. In our previous paper, the robot is simplified with spheres, and the distances between the spheres and voxels are computed with the hypot function using their center positions. Such distance checking with a simplified model can run almost in real-time. However, due to the simplification the computed distances are smaller than the actual values, which makes the robot's behavior conservative and reduces its productivity. In contrast, an exact mesh-to-mesh distance checker cannot run in real-time (experimentally, 130 \mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro s} per configuration and 65 \mathrm{m}\mathrm{s} per trajectory with FCL [3]). To the best of our knowledge, no existing distance checker is applicable to real-time safety control.

In this paper, we propose a batched, fast and precise distance checker based on pre-computed link-local Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) to address this issue. By leveraging GPU parallelization for the pre-processing of the robot's SDFs, the proposed method can check distances for multiple robot configurations within less than 1 \mathrm{m}\mathrm{s} at runtime. We additionally propose a neural approximation of the pre-processing, which results in 2x faster pre-processing. Finally, we experimentally demonstrate that our distance checker navigates a robot faster than the method using a robot modeled with spheres in a dynamic, collaborative environment.

The paper is organized as follows. Section II surveys related work. Section III presents our parallel distance checking method and some techniques to reduce the pre-processing time in a constant order, including the neural approximation. In Section IV, we evaluate the performance of the neural approximation and examine whether the approximation affects the precision of distance computation; we then show the experimental comparison for real-time safe path tracking in a collaborative environment. Finally, in Section V we discuss the limitations of our approach and conclude with some directions for future work.

References:
[1] Shohei Fujii and Quang-Cuong Pham. Time-Optimal Path Tracking with ISO Safety Guarantees. In 2023 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS) , pages 5926–5933, October 2023.
[2] ISO/TS 15066. Robots and robotic devices collaborative robots, 2016.
[3] J. Pan, S. Chitta, and D. Manocha. FCL: A general purpose library for collision and proximity queries. In 2012 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation , pages 3859–3866, 2012.
